topic: Pilates for shoulder rehab

slides.headline: Shoulder rehab stuck at the band stage?
slides.sub: How clinical Pilates can bridge the gap back to full use.

slides.title: Where Pilates fits in shoulder rehab
slides.body: Once the early stage of rehab is under way, Pilates can help build the strength and control your shoulder needs for daily life. It sits alongside your rehab plan, not instead of it.

slides.title: Springs let you load gradually
slides.body: Reformer springs can support part of your arm's weight or add resistance in small steps. That makes it easier to find a level that challenges the shoulder without stirring up a flare-up.

slides.title: Train the shoulder blade too
slides.body: Your shoulder blade is the base your arm works from. Rows, arm work on the reformer and side-lying exercises help the shoulder blade and rotator cuff muscles share the load.

slides.title: Reach overhead, one step at a time
slides.body: Reaching overhead is often the last thing to come back. Your instructor can build range gradually, starting with support and progressing as the shoulder settles and gets stronger.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A shoulder that suddenly can't lift after a fall, pain with pins and needles down the arm, or night pain that keeps building is worth reviewing with your physio or GP.

slides.headline: Ready to build your shoulder back up?
slides.body: Our Pilates team starts with an assessment, works within any physio or surgeon guidelines and builds sessions around your shoulder. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Shoulder rehab stuck at the resistance band stage?

Bands are a great start, but many people reach a point where the shoulder needs more varied, progressive load to handle everyday life again: hanging washing, lifting bags into the car, reaching for the top shelf.

That's where clinical Pilates can help. Reformer springs can support or challenge your arm in small steps, and the work covers the shoulder blade and rotator cuff as well as the arm itself. If you've had surgery or are seeing a physio, your sessions follow their plan.

topic: What your chiropractor checks before an adjustment

slides.headline: Before the adjustment: what we check
slides.sub: Why your first chiro visit starts with questions, not a quick click.

slides.title: Your story comes first
slides.body: Expect questions about when the pain started, what eases it, what makes it worse, your work, your sport and your general health. It shapes everything that follows, so share the details.

slides.title: Screening for red flags
slides.body: Your chiropractor will ask about things like unexplained weight loss, fever, numbness, bladder or bowel changes and recent trauma. Most people have none of these, but checking is part of safe care.

slides.title: Movement and nerve checks
slides.body: You'll usually be asked to bend, turn and move. Reflex, strength and sensation checks help show whether nerves are involved and which areas are stiff or sensitive.

slides.title: Is an adjustment right today?
slides.body: Adjustments aren't right for everyone or every visit. Depending on what's found, your chiropractor may use soft tissue work, mobilisation or exercise instead, or refer you to your GP or a physio.

slides.title: You can always say no
slides.body: Your chiropractor should explain what they plan to do and why, then ask for your consent. If you'd prefer a gentler technique, or no adjustment at all, just say so.

slides.headline: Curious what an assessment involves?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess before they treat and explain your options in plain English, with exercise as part of the plan. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Ever wondered why your chiropractor asks so many questions before doing anything?

A good adjustment starts well before anyone touches your spine. Your history, a few screening questions and some simple movement and nerve checks help your chiropractor decide what's likely going on and what's appropriate for you.

Sometimes that means an adjustment. Sometimes it means soft tissue work, mobilisation, exercises, or a referral to your GP or one of our physios. And you're always welcome to ask questions or say no to any technique.

topic: Beach gear, eskies and your back

slides.headline: Loaded esky, long walk to the sand?
slides.sub: A few ways to get your beach gear there without a grumpy back.

slides.title: Split the load in two
slides.body: One heavy esky in one hand leaves you leaning to the side for the whole walk. Two smaller bags, one in each hand, or a backpack spreads the load and keeps you more upright.

slides.title: Wheels are your friend
slides.body: A beach trolley or an esky with wheels saves a lot of carrying across the car park. On soft sand, pulling it behind you is usually easier than pushing it.

slides.title: Lift the esky like a deadlift
slides.body: Stand close with feet apart, bend at your knees and hips, keep the esky near your body and stand up smoothly. When lifting it from the boot, turn with your feet, not your back.

slides.title: Two trips beat one heroic one
slides.body: Carrying the umbrella, chairs, towels and esky in one go is tempting. Two lighter trips across the sand usually feel easier on your back than one overloaded walk in the heat.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: If back pain after a big beach day spreads down a leg, comes with numbness or weakness, or isn't starting to settle after a few days, it's worth getting it assessed.

slides.headline: Back grumbling after beach days?
slides.body: Our chiropractors look at how you move and lift, then combine hands-on care with simple exercises. Book online via the link in bio.

A few small changes help: split the load between two hands or a backpack, use wheels wherever you can, lift the esky close to your body with bent knees, and take two lighter trips instead of one big one.

topic: Kayaking and paddleboarding: shoulders and back

slides.headline: Kayak or SUP day on the cards?
slides.sub: How to keep your shoulders and back happy out on the water.

slides.title: Power comes from your trunk
slides.body: Whether you're in a kayak or on a paddleboard, rotating through your trunk shares the work with bigger muscles. Pulling with your arms alone tires the shoulders quickly and often leaves them sore.

slides.title: Keep the paddle close
slides.body: Reaching far out to the side puts your shoulder in a weaker position. Keep strokes close to the board or boat, with your top hand around eye height rather than high overhead.

slides.title: Soft knees on the board
slides.body: On a paddleboard, stand with feet hip-width apart and knees slightly bent. Locked knees push more work into your lower back. Kneeling for a while is a handy break.

slides.title: Build up your time on the water
slides.body: Your first paddle of summer isn't the time for a three-hour trip. Start with 30 to 45 minutes, take breaks, and build up over a few outings as your shoulders adapt.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Shoulder pain that wakes you at night, weakness lifting your arm, pins and needles in the hand, or back pain spreading down a leg is worth assessing rather than paddling through.

slides.headline: Sore after your last paddle?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios assess your shoulder and back, then build a plan to get you paddling comfortably again. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Paddled out feeling great, drove home with sore shoulders and a stiff back?

Kayaking and paddleboarding are fantastic summer exercise, but the first few outings often ask more of your shoulders and back than they're used to.

A few tweaks usually help: turn through your trunk rather than pulling with your arms, keep the paddle close to the board, soften your knees on a SUP, and build up your time on the water over several trips instead of starting with a marathon.

slides.title: Training load does the most
slides.body: Pre-season usually means more running, sprints and gym in a short space of time. Heavy legs are common. Sleep, food and sensible load planning do most of the recovery work.

slides.title: Where massage can help
slides.body: Massage can help muscles feel looser and ease that heavy, tight feeling for a while. Many players find it helps them move more comfortably into the next session.

slides.body: Firmer work often suits a day or two before a big session, not the night before. After a heavy block of training, lighter pressure usually feels better than deep work.

slides.title: Massage doesn't replace rehab

topic: Walking for back pain: how much and how fast

slides.headline: Back pain? Let's talk walking
slides.sub: How far, how fast and how often, in plain terms.

slides.title: Why walking often helps
slides.body: Walking gently moves your spine, gets blood flowing and can help calm sensitive tissues. Current guidelines encourage staying active with back pain, and walking is one of the easiest ways to do it.

slides.title: Start where it feels OK
slides.body: Find a distance or time you can walk with only mild, manageable discomfort. For some people that's five minutes, for others it's thirty. That's your starting point, not a failure.

slides.title: Short and often beats one long walk
slides.body: Two or three 10-minute walks spread through the day are often easier than one 30-minute effort. Add a few minutes every few days if your back is handling it well.

slides.title: Pace: relaxed but purposeful
slides.body: A natural pace with your arms swinging often feels easier on a sore back than a slow, stiff shuffle. You should still be able to talk. Speed can build as you improve.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, leg weakness, fever or unexplained weight loss need prompt medical attention. Back pain that isn't easing after a few weeks is worth assessing.

slides.headline: Want a walking plan for your back?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios can map out a walking and exercise plan that suits your back and your week. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Told to 'keep walking' with back pain, but nobody said how much?

Walking is one of the simplest ways to stay active with a sore back. The trick is finding your starting point: a time or distance you can manage with only mild discomfort, even if that's five minutes.

From there, short and frequent walks usually beat one long one. Add a few minutes every few days, keep a relaxed pace with your arms swinging, and in the summer heat aim for early mornings or evenings.

topic: Pilates for knee rehab

slides.headline: Knee rehab: where Pilates fits in
slides.sub: Building strength around a sore or recovering knee, one spring at a time.

slides.title: It builds on your rehab plan
slides.body: Pilates for a knee is most useful as part of a bigger rehab plan. If you've had surgery, your surgeon's protocol and your physio set the rules, and your Pilates sessions follow them.

slides.title: Load without the impact
slides.body: Footwork on the reformer lets you press through your legs while lying down, with springs setting the load. It's a handy way to build quad and calf strength before more impact.

slides.title: Hips and ankles matter too
slides.body: Knees often work harder when the hips and ankles aren't pulling their weight. Bridges, side-lying leg work and calf raises train the whole leg, not just the knee.

slides.title: Control on one leg
slides.body: Single-leg work, like single-leg presses or slow step-downs, helps the knee cope with real life: stairs, getting out of the car and changing direction. Slow and steady beats fast and wobbly.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A knee that swells quickly, locks, gives way, or becomes hot and red is worth reviewing with your physio or GP before you continue your program.

slides.headline: Want your knee working with you again?
slides.body: Our Pilates team assesses your knee, works within any surgeon or physio guidelines and progresses you gradually. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Knee feeling better, but not quite trustworthy on the stairs yet?

That in-between stage is where clinical Pilates can be useful. Reformer footwork lets you build leg strength with springs setting the load, and the program can work the hips and ankles too, since they share the job with your knee.

Single-leg control comes next, so the knee is ready for stairs, uneven ground and getting in and out of the car. If you've had surgery, your surgeon's protocol and your physio's plan always come first.

topic: Massage for tradies: shoulders, forearms and lower back

slides.title: Shoulders from overhead work
slides.body: Hours of drilling, painting or installing overhead can leave your shoulders and upper back tight and tired. Massage around the shoulder blades and neck can ease that tension for a while.

slides.title: Forearms that grip all day
slides.body: Tools, drills and ladders mean constant gripping. Forearm and hand work can ease that tight, achy feeling, and gentle wrist and finger stretches between jobs help keep it in check.

slides.title: Lower back from bending and lifting
slides.body: Lifting, kneeling and bending over benches adds up across a week. Massage to the lower back, glutes and hips can help things feel easier to move, especially after a big stretch of work.

topic: Strength training after 50: getting started

slides.headline: Over 50 and never lifted a weight?
slides.sub: Strength is trainable at any age. Here's a simple way to start.

slides.title: Why strength matters more now
slides.body: Muscle and bone keep responding to load throughout life. Research suggests strength training can help with everyday tasks, balance and joint pain, and it's rarely too late to start.

slides.title: Pick four or five basic moves
slides.body: Sit-to-stands, wall push-ups, step-ups, band rows and calf raises cover most of the body. You don't need a gym to begin, just a chair, a step and a resistance band.

slides.title: Twice a week is a great start
slides.body: Two sessions a week of 20 to 30 minutes is enough for most people to feel a difference. Aim for 8 to 12 reps, where the last few feel challenging but controlled.

slides.title: Some stiffness is normal
slides.body: Feeling a bit stiff a day or two later is common when you start. If a joint aches, adjust the load or range rather than stopping altogether, and progress over weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Chest pain, dizziness or unusual breathlessness with exercise needs a GP review. If a joint swells or pain builds session after session, see a physio to adjust your program.

slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios build strength programs around your joints, your history and your goals. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: Is it normal to feel sore after an adjustment?

slides.headline: A bit sore after your adjustment?
slides.sub: What's common, how long it lasts and when to get in touch.

slides.title: Mild soreness is common
slides.body: Some people feel achy or stiff for a day or so after an adjustment, a bit like after a new workout. It usually settles on its own within 24 to 48 hours.

slides.title: Why it happens
slides.body: Joints and muscles that haven't moved much for a while are being asked to do something different. Your nervous system may respond with some short-term sensitivity, especially after a first visit.

slides.title: What helps in the meantime
slides.body: Keep moving gently, go for a walk and try heat if it feels good. Avoid long periods in one position, and do your home exercises at an easy level.

slides.title: Tell your chiropractor
slides.body: Let your chiropractor know how you felt after the last visit. They can change the technique, use gentler options, or focus more on exercise and soft tissue work next time.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Soreness that keeps building after 48 hours, new numbness or weakness, a severe headache, dizziness or vision changes need prompt attention. Contact your chiropractor or GP, or call 000 in an emergency.

slides.headline: Questions about your last visit?
slides.body: Our chiropractors explain what to expect around each session, and adjust care to how you respond. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Felt a bit stiff the day after your chiro visit? You're not the only one.

Mild soreness after an adjustment is fairly common, especially after a first visit. It often feels like the ache after a new workout and usually settles within a day or two.

Gentle movement, a walk and a bit of heat tend to help more than resting on the couch. And let your chiropractor know how you felt, because it helps them tailor the next session. Anything that keeps building, or new numbness, weakness, dizziness or a severe headache, needs prompt attention.

topic: When we'll suggest seeing your GP

slides.headline: When we'll send you to your GP
slides.sub: Good care includes knowing when something needs a doctor as well.

slides.title: We work alongside your GP
slides.body: Physios, chiropractors and remedial massage therapists see lots of aches and pains that settle with movement and time. Some situations need a doctor as well, and we'll say so clearly.

slides.title: Signs that need medical input
slides.body: Fever with back pain, unexplained weight loss, night pain that doesn't ease in any position, or feeling generally unwell alongside pain are reasons we'll ask you to see your GP.

slides.title: Nerve changes worth acting on
slides.body: Numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, or leg weakness that's getting worse need urgent medical care. We'll direct you to your GP or the emergency department straight away.

slides.title: When progress stalls
slides.body: If you're doing the work and things aren't improving over several weeks, a GP review can look at other factors, consider tests if appropriate, and talk through other options with you.

slides.title: It's not a brush-off
slides.body: Suggesting a GP visit doesn't mean we're stepping away. With your consent we can write to your GP, keep treating when it's appropriate and work together on your plan.

topic: Grip strength and healthy ageing

slides.headline: How strong is your grip, really?
slides.sub: It's about more than opening jars. Here's how to train it.

slides.title: More than a party trick
slides.body: Research suggests grip strength is linked with overall strength and how well people manage everyday life as they age. It isn't the whole story, but it's a handy, simple marker.

slides.title: Everyday signs to notice
slides.body: Struggling with jar lids, carrying shopping bags or holding a heavy pan can hint that your grip could use some work. Many people only notice when a task starts to feel hard.

slides.title: Carry things on purpose
slides.body: Farmer's carries are simple: hold a heavy bag or dumbbell in each hand and walk for 30 seconds. Shopping bags from the car count too, if you stand tall and take your time.

slides.title: Squeeze, pinch and hang
slides.body: Squeeze a soft ball or rolled towel, pinch two weight plates together, or hang briefly from a bar with your feet on the ground. Two or three times a week is plenty.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Weakness in one hand, pins and needles, dropping things more often, or swollen, painful finger joints are all worth a proper assessment rather than more squeezing at home.

slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios can check your strength and build a simple program that fits your week. Book online via the link in bio.

topic: How long do the effects of a massage last?

slides.headline: How long does that looser feeling last?
slides.sub: The honest answer about massage, and how to make it go further.

slides.title: Usually hours to a few days
slides.body: Most people feel looser and more relaxed for somewhere between a few hours and a few days. It varies with your body, stress, sleep and what you do afterwards.

slides.title: Why the effect fades
slides.body: Massage mainly changes how muscles and nerves feel, rather than changing tissue for good. If the habits that built the tightness come back, the tightness often does too.

slides.title: Move while it feels easier
slides.body: The window after a massage is a great time to move. A walk, some gentle mobility or your home exercises that evening can help you hold onto that easier feeling.

slides.title: Change the daily load
slides.body: If your shoulders tighten after every long desk day, small changes like regular breaks and a strength routine often do more to extend the effect than booking more often.

slides.title: Find a rhythm that suits you
slides.body: Some people book every few weeks in busy seasons and less often otherwise. Your remedial massage therapist can help you work out what's realistic for your goals and budget.

slides.headline: Want your massage to go further?
slides.body: Our remedial massage therapists pair hands-on work with simple things you can do between sessions. Book online via the link in bio.

Walked out of your massage feeling brand new, then two days later the tight shoulders were back?

That's pretty normal. For most people, the looser, calmer feeling lasts somewhere between a few hours and a few days. Massage changes how your muscles and nerves feel, and if the same habits keep loading you up, the tightness tends to return.

The good news: you can stretch that window. Move while things feel easier, keep up any home exercises, and look at the daily load, like long unbroken desk stretches, that keeps winding you up.

topic: Pilates for footballers: hamstrings and groin

slides.headline: Footy prep: hamstrings and groin
slides.sub: How Pilates can build strength where footballers often get caught out.

slides.title: Why these two cop it
slides.body: Sprinting, kicking and changing direction put big demands on the hamstrings and groin. Strains in these areas are common in football, especially when training load jumps quickly.

slides.title: Hamstrings need long strength
slides.body: Hamstrings often get hurt at speed while they're lengthening. Reformer work like hamstring curls, bridges and slow single-leg exercises can help build strength through a longer range.

slides.title: Train the inner thigh too
slides.body: Your adductors control your legs when you kick and cut. Side-lying work, squeeze exercises and side planks with the top leg supported build the groin strength footballers often miss.

slides.title: An add-on, not a swap
slides.body: Pilates is most useful alongside running and gym work, not instead of them. One or two sessions a week in pre-season and a lighter dose during the season suits most players.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A sharp pain mid-sprint, bruising, pain when walking, or groin pain that keeps returning after games is worth a physio assessment before you load it further.

slides.headline: Want stronger legs for next season?
slides.body: Our Pilates team builds sessions around your position, training week and past strains, working with our physios when needed. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Hamstrings and groin: the two spots footballers most often end up talking about on the sideline.

Sprinting, kicking and quick changes of direction ask a lot of both, and strains often turn up when training load jumps in pre-season.

topic: Carrying luggage through airports: back-friendly travel

slides.headline: Airport lugging leaving your back sore?
slides.sub: Easy ways to handle suitcases, carry-ons and overhead lockers this summer.

slides.title: Four wheels beat two
slides.body: Spinner cases roll beside you, so you can push rather than drag a bag behind with a twisted arm. Swap hands every so often so one side isn't doing all the work.

slides.title: Lift from the carousel calmly
slides.body: Wait until your bag comes close, step towards it, bend your knees and use the handle. Pull it towards you before lifting, rather than yanking it off at arm's length.

slides.title: Overhead lockers in two steps
slides.body: Lift your carry-on to the seat back or armrest first, then up into the locker. Keep it close to your body and face the locker rather than twisting.

slides.title: Pack lighter where you can
slides.body: Every kilo counts when you lift a bag five or six times per trip. Heavy items packed at the wheel end keep the case balanced and easier to tip and roll.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain after travel that spreads down a leg, comes with numbness or weakness, or isn't easing a few days after you get home is worth getting assessed.

topic: The sit-to-stand test: a quick leg strength check

slides.headline: Can you stand up 5 times, no hands?
slides.sub: A simple chair test that tells you a lot about your legs.

slides.title: How to do the test
slides.body: Use a firm chair against a wall. Sit with your arms crossed over your chest. Stand up fully and sit back down five times as quickly as you safely can, and time it.

slides.title: What your time can suggest
slides.body: A quicker time usually means stronger, more powerful legs. A slower time, or needing your hands, suggests your legs could use some training. It's a check-in, not a diagnosis.

slides.title: Stay safe while you test
slides.body: Have someone nearby if your balance isn't great, and skip it if you feel dizzy or have a very sore knee or hip. Stop straight away if anything feels sharp.

slides.title: Turn the test into training
slides.body: Sit-to-stands are also a great exercise. Try three sets of 8 to 10 on most days. Make it harder with a lower chair, a slower lowering or holding a weight.

slides.title: Retest every month
slides.body: Write down your time and repeat the test every four weeks. Watching it improve is motivating, and a slower time is useful information to share with your physio.

topic: Is Pilates enough strength training?

slides.headline: Is Pilates enough to keep you strong?
slides.sub: An honest look at what Pilates builds and where it might fall short.

slides.title: Pilates does build strength
slides.body: Reformer springs and body-weight work challenge your muscles, especially around the trunk, hips and shoulders. For many people, that's a real step up from doing no strength work at all.

slides.title: Where it can fall short
slides.body: Springs top out at a certain resistance, and a lot of Pilates is done lying down. Heavier loads, like lifting weights, may add more for bone and muscle over time.

slides.title: It depends on your goal
slides.body: If you want to move better, feel stronger and manage a back niggle, Pilates may be plenty. If you want to lift heavier or build bone strength, adding weights can help.

slides.title: Make your sessions count
slides.body: Ask your instructor to progress springs and reps as you improve. Include standing and single-leg work, not just exercises on your back. The last few reps should feel genuinely challenging.

slides.title: Pair Pilates with weights
slides.body: A mix works well for many people: one or two Pilates sessions for control and mobility, plus one weights session for heavier load. Our team can help you plan the week.

topic: Shoulder pain at night: sleeping positions that help

slides.headline: Shoulder waking you up at 2am?
slides.sub: Sleeping positions that often make a sore shoulder easier to live with.

slides.title: Why nights are harder
slides.body: When you lie down, sensitive shoulder tissues can get squashed or stretched, and there's less to distract you. Night pain is common with many shoulder problems and often eases as things settle.

slides.title: On your back, with support
slides.body: Lie on your back with a pillow under the sore arm, so it rests slightly out from your side. This stops the shoulder dropping backwards into an uncomfortable position.

slides.title: On the good side, hug a pillow
slides.body: If you're a side sleeper, lie on the other side and hug a pillow against your chest. Resting the sore arm on it stops it falling forward across your body.

slides.title: Skip the arm-under-pillow habit
slides.body: Sleeping with your arm tucked under your head or pillow keeps it raised for hours. It feels comfortable at first, but many people find it stirs up a sore shoulder.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Night pain that keeps getting worse, a shoulder you can't lift after a fall, fever, or pain with pins and needles down the arm is worth assessing promptly.

slides.headline: Want a better night's sleep?

topic: Cracking your own neck: is it OK?

slides.headline: Always cracking your own neck?
slides.sub: Is it a problem, and what might your neck actually want instead?

slides.title: The sound itself is usually harmless
slides.body: That pop is usually gas bubbles changing in the joint fluid, not bones moving back into place. Most people who crack their own neck now and then don't come to any harm.

slides.title: Why the urge keeps coming back
slides.body: The relief is often short-lived because the stiffness comes from somewhere else, like long hours in one position or tight surrounding muscles. So you crack again, and again.

slides.title: Gentle, never forceful
slides.body: Avoid sharp, forceful twists or pushing your head with your hands. If you move your neck for relief, slow turns and tilts within a comfortable range are a gentler choice.

slides.title: Try movement instead
slides.body: Chin tucks, shoulder rolls and slow head turns every hour or so often ease that urge. Building upper back and neck strength can help your neck feel less stiff overall.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Dizziness, a severe or unusual headache, blurred vision, trouble speaking or numbness after neck movement need urgent medical attention. Call 000 if symptoms are sudden or severe.

topic: Pilates with knee or hip osteoarthritis

slides.headline: Pilates with an arthritic knee or hip?
slides.sub: Why moving the joint is usually part of the answer, not the problem.

slides.title: Joints like to move
slides.body: Current guidelines recommend exercise as a first-line approach for knee and hip osteoarthritis. Regular movement can help ease stiffness and pain, and keep you doing the things you enjoy.

slides.title: Why Pilates suits many people
slides.body: Reformer springs let you start with support and less body weight, then build up gradually. Many exercises are done lying or sitting, which can suit sore or stiff days.

slides.title: Strength around the joint
slides.body: Strong quads, glutes and calves help share the load around an arthritic knee or hip. Footwork, bridges, side-lying leg work and supported squats are common starting points.

slides.title: Some ache is OK
slides.body: Mild discomfort during exercise that settles within a day is usually fine. If pain is much worse the next morning, your instructor can reduce the load and progress more gradually.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A joint that becomes hot, red and very swollen, locks or gives way, or pain that keeps you awake at night is worth reviewing with your physio or GP.

topic: Packing the car for a holiday road trip

slides.headline: Packing the car for a road trip?
slides.sub: A few loading habits that make the first leg easier on your back.

slides.title: Heavy bags in first
slides.body: Load the heaviest bags first, close to the back seats, so you're not reaching over them later. Bend your knees, bring each bag close and slide it in rather than swinging it.

slides.title: Don't lean deep into the boot
slides.body: Leaning far into the boot with a heavy bag at arm's length is a classic back tweak. Step in close, rest the bag on the bumper edge first, then slide it into place.

slides.title: Smaller bags, more trips
slides.body: One enormous bag is tempting but awkward to lift. Several medium bags are easier to handle and pack more neatly. An extra walk to the car is a small price.

slides.title: Set your seat before you go
slides.body: Sit close enough to reach the pedals with a slight bend in your knees, with your back supported by the seat. Set your mirrors once you're sitting well, so you don't slump later.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Back pain after packing that spreads down a leg, comes with numbness or weakness, or isn't easing after a few days is worth getting assessed.

topic: Tummy gap after pregnancy (abdominal separation)

slides.headline: Tummy gap after having a baby?
slides.sub: Abdominal separation is really common. Here's what usually helps.

slides.title: Common and a normal change
slides.body: Your tummy muscles stretch apart during pregnancy to make room for your baby. Most people have some separation after birth, and for many it narrows over the first few months.

slides.title: Function matters more than the gap
slides.body: The width of the gap isn't the whole story. How well your tummy muscles support you during everyday tasks often matters more than exactly how wide the gap measures.

slides.title: Start with breathing and gentle work
slides.body: Gentle breathing, pelvic floor and deep tummy exercises are usually a good starting point. Your physio can guide you on when to progress to more challenging core work.

slides.title: Everyday habits that help
slides.body: Roll onto your side to get out of bed, breathe out as you lift your baby or the pram, and try not to hold your breath when you strain. Small changes add up.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A bulge that doesn't settle, pain around the gap, ongoing back pain, leaking, or a feeling of heaviness in the pelvic area is worth assessing with your physio or GP.
